title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Mill and Its Shadows

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

I'm your host, and over the course of this series we're going to live inside one of the great novels of the English language — George Eliot's extraordinary story of Maggie Tulliver, her brother Tom, and the river that shapes and finally claims them both.
This is a novel about intelligence that has nowhere to go, about love that cannot quite find its right object, and about the crushing weight of family, duty, and provincial life.
It is also — and this matters — one of the funniest, most sharply observed novels ever written in English.
With me today are three guests who know this book intimately and argue about it with genuine heat.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing scholar whose obsession is with how great writers construct their effects — the architecture beneath the surface of the prose.
She has an extraordinary gift for making technical craft feel genuinely thrilling, and The Mill on the Floss is, I think it's fair to say, one of her touchstone texts.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don — a man who reads novels as moral investigations, as stories about individual character tested to its limits.
He is beautifully spoken, occasionally withering, and always a reminder that great fiction is first and last about human goodness and its costs.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive — comes to every novel as a performer.
He hears what the prose is doing, spots the comic timing, and reads with a relish that makes the text sound like it was written yesterday.
Welcome, all three of you.
Let's begin where the novel really begins — not with the river, not with the mill, but with Maggie Tulliver herself, and that extraordinary, restless, hungry mind of hers.
What strikes me every time I return to this novel is how early Eliot establishes the core tragedy — and she does it through comedy.
There's that wonderful scene with Maggie and the Latin Grammar — Tom's Latin Grammar, which supposedly no girls can learn.
And Maggie, of course, finds it immediately absorbing — she skips straight past the rules to the examples.
Eliot's description of what captivates her is one of the most precise accounts of a certain kind of literary imagination I've ever read.
She sets it up so carefully before she gives you the image — listen to this.
"These mysterious sentences, snatched from an unknown context,—like strange horns of beasts, and leaves of unknown plants, brought from some far-off region,—gave boundless scope to her imagination."
Strange horns of beasts, leaves of unknown plants — that is a child's mind working at full stretch.
And the sorrow built into the comedy is that this magnificent instrument is going to be given absolutely nothing adequate to work on.
I take your point about comedy, Eleanor, though I think we should be careful not to let structural admiration muffle the moral substance.
What Eliot is showing us — and she is perfectly clear about it — is a child who is proud because she found the Latin interesting.
That little detail — she was proud because she found it interesting — is a portrait of a virtue: the love of learning for its own sake.
What the novel will track, with what I can only call merciless tenderness, is whether that virtue can survive what life does to it.
What I love — and Edmund has touched on it without quite saying it — is the specific detail of how Maggie approaches the Grammar.
She finds the English Key at the end, which will make her very wise about Latin at slight expense — that phrase, slight expense, is pure comedy.
Eliot knows exactly what a ten-year-old autodidact looks like — cutting straight to the answers, skipping the rules.
And then she gets lost in the thick grove penetrable by no star — and Tom calls out.
The interruption is perfect timing.
And that interruption by Tom haunts the whole novel, doesn't it.
But there is another relationship that begins in childhood which is subtler, and stranger, and perhaps even more revealing about Maggie's emotional life.
Her early friendship with Philip Wakem — the lawyer's son, the boy with the crooked back.
The Philip scenes are where Eliot's craft becomes almost painfully refined.
Philip is drawn to Maggie with an intensity that even as children carries the weight of adult longing.
And the question he asks her — the question about whether she would have loved him as well as Tom if he had been her brother — is one of the most quietly devastating lines in the book.
He is asking: could you have loved me, had you been obliged to?
Philip's declaration later is what I keep returning to.
It has a gravity quite unlike anything else in the early chapters — a boy speaking with a man's grief already formed in him.
Eliot gives him this:
"I'm very fond of you, Maggie; I shall never forget you. And when I'm very unhappy, I shall always think of you, and wish I had a sister with dark eyes, just like yours."
A child saying that he expects to be very unhappy — and that his consolation will be imaginary.
That is not sentimentality; that is moral clairvoyance.
When I read Philip aloud, I have to hold myself back from making him too poignant too soon.
Because Eliot does something rather brilliant — she lets Maggie respond with absolute, uncomplicated warmth.
Wondering how to convince Philip that she could like him just as well, despite his deformity, she says — and this is just as written:
"Should you like me to kiss you, as I do Tom? I will, if you like."
There is no guile in it whatsoever.
It is the purest possible expression of a generous heart that doesn't yet know how complicated love is going to become.
That innocence is precisely what makes what follows so hard to bear.
We've seen Maggie's mind ignite over a Latin Grammar, and her heart open instinctively toward someone the world will teach her to keep at a distance.
In our next segment, we'll look at the forces ranged against her — the family, the town, and a social world that has very precise ideas about what a girl like Maggie is permitted to become.

segments.title: The Weight of Inheritance: Mr. Tulliver's Downfall

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked, the programme where we take George Eliot's great novel apart sentence by sentence and ask how it works — and why it endures.
Today's segment takes us to the heart of the novel's first catastrophe: the ruin of Mr Tulliver, the proud, hot-headed miller of Dorlcote.
With me are three readers who bring very different lenses to this material.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing scholar whose great gift is showing us how the machinery of a great prose sentence actually works.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose allegiance is to the moral imagination of fiction — to questions of character, goodness, and the wages of pride.
And Oliver Trevelyan is the man who has read more classic novels aloud than almost anyone alive — and who hears the rhythms of Eliot's prose as music as much as meaning.
We begin with the forces that drive Tulliver toward his lawsuit — the fatal combination of a nagging wife, a hated enemy, and his own magnificent stubbornness.
What strikes me first about these chapters is how Eliot distributes blame with almost mathematical precision.
She is entirely unwilling to let any single cause carry the weight of the disaster.
And the instrument she uses to make that argument is one of the most quietly devastating metaphors in the novel.
She writes that Mrs Tulliver's pleading might be comparable to
But Eliot refuses to stop there — she immediately redistributes blame onto, as she puts it, the previous weight of feathers.
It is a comic image doing tragic structural work — the whole system of accumulated pressures that made Tulliver so explosively fragile.
Eleanor is right to flag that passage, and I would add that Eliot's satirical intelligence here is deployed in the service of a deeper moral observation.
What she is describing, beneath the comedy of the camel and the feather, is a man who has surrendered his will to a cluster of resentments.
And chief among those resentments is his hatred of Wakem — which is not merely personal but almost mythological in its intensity.
Eliot tells us, with her characteristic deadpan, that Wakem's rascality was of a peculiarly aggravated kind — the kind that placed itself in opposition to Mr Tulliver's interests and opinions.
That is the comic sting, of course — that the definition of injustice in Tulliver's mind is whatever inconveniences him personally.
It is the portrait of a man whose honest self-belief has curdled, under pressure, into something very close to monomania.
Edmund, you're absolutely right about the monomania — and the extraordinary thing is that Eliot manages to make it hilarious and pitiable at the same moment.
Because listen to how she renders Tulliver's own inner voice when he thinks about Wakem.
She gives us this magnificent burst of colloquial venom:
As a performer, that sentence is a gift — the rhythm of it, the contempt packed into 'cool as a cucumber.'
It sounds exactly like a man talking to himself in a fury — and that is precisely what Eliot intends.
And yet for all the comedy of Tulliver's hatred, his philosophy of the law is not entirely absurd — Eliot takes care to give it its own twisted logic.
Eleanor, that passage about the cock-fight seems to me one of the great compressed satirical strokes in the whole novel.
It is extraordinary, isn't it — two sentences carrying a whole critique of the legal system.
And the key is that Eliot affirms his honesty before she dismantles his reasoning.
She writes, with complete seriousness, that Mr Tulliver was a strictly honest man, and proud of being honest.
But then — the pivot — she tells us he believed that justice in law could only be achieved by employing a stronger knave to frustrate a weaker.
And then comes the image that crystallises it all:
There is the whole corruption laid bare — honesty that has philosophically accommodated itself to the very knavery it despises.
Eleanor puts it well, and I think one must not miss the tragic dimension lurking inside the satire.
Tulliver is not a hypocrite in the ordinary sense — he genuinely cannot see the contradiction.
And that moral blindness — which is also a kind of innocence — is precisely what makes him destructible.
Eliot's genius is to make us laugh at the cock-fight metaphor even as we sense the cliff approaching.
And that cliff, as Edmund calls it — there's also this brilliant digression on education that tells us the whole world Tulliver inhabits is equally corrupt, equally blind.
The passage about Mr Stelling and the clergymen-schoolmasters is Eliot in full polemical flight — and it is tremendously funny.
She asks, with perfect mock-innocence, how these underpaid clergymen were to survive.
And then delivers the verdict:
The audacity of that construction — 'was it their fault' — is breathtaking.
She is indicting an entire class structure while appearing to defend one hapless clergyman.
What I love about that passage is the boarding-school prospectus buried in the comedy — 'including the return of linen, fork, and spoon.'
That detail is doing double duty — it's absurdly specific and it perfectly captures the anxious consumerism of these fathers buying education the way they'd buy a service.
And Tulliver is exactly that father — well-meaning, proud, entirely at the mercy of a system he cannot read.
And then the comedy stops entirely — because all of this accumulating pressure, these feathers on the camel's back, finally breaks him.
Edmund — the moment when Maggie tells Tom what has happened — what do you make of Eliot's handling of that scene?
It is one of the great tonal pivots in the novel — and it comes with very little preparation, which is precisely the point.
The satire simply ceases, and we are left with a child carrying devastating news to her brother.
Eliot gives Maggie the words in a rush — as if, she writes, the words would burst from her.
The simplicity of those words — nothing ornate, nothing philosophical — is shattering after all the irony that preceded it.
'He will have nothing left' — four words, and a world collapses.
And it gets darker still — because it isn't only the mill and the land.
Maggie also has to tell Tom what has happened to their father himself.
And Eliot renders that in Maggie's own fractured, almost dissociated speech:
When I read that aloud, I always drop my voice on 'O father, father' — because it is no longer narration, it is pure grief escaping the frame of the sentence.
The man who was going to beat the Dodsons, who was going to employ the best spurred game bird in the cock-fight — he knows nobody.
Only Maggie.
That moment — 'he has known nobody but me ever since' — is where the novel's whole architecture of satire and irony earns its emotional payout.
All the comedy of the feather and the camel, of the cock-fight, of the incompetent clergyman-schoolmaster — it was building toward this grief.
Eliot never lets you forget that behind every satirical target there is a person — and that person can be broken.
And it is Maggie who knows him still — which tells us something essential about where the novel is heading.
Thank you all — that was a remarkable examination of how Eliot constructs a fall: from satirical diagnosis, through comic accumulation, to the bare grief of a daughter's voice.
We'll be back after the break to follow Maggie through the ruins of that inheritance.

segments.title: A Girl's Forbidden Mind: Maggie's Hunger for Knowledge

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're looking at one of the most compelling child portraits in all of Victorian fiction: Maggie Tulliver's fierce, ungovernable hunger for knowledge and experience.

A girl who reads the dictionary for pleasure, deduces the meaning of Greek prefixes at age eight, and fantasises about running away to the gypsies — because at least there she might be respected for her superior knowledge.
Joining me are three guests who bring very different lenses to bear on George Eliot's remarkable creation.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a literary critic and novelist whose eye for craft — for what a sentence is actually doing — makes her indispensable when we're reading Eliot at full stretch.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads great fiction as moral drama — stories about character tested by circumstance, about goodness and the weakness of will.

And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and the voice of more classic audiobooks than I dare count — he comes to every novel as a performer, hearing the rhythms, catching the comic timing, knowing when the prose is written for the voice.
Let's begin with Maggie's mind itself — that extraordinary, self-assembled, lopsided intelligence.
What strikes me first is Eliot's audacity in the narrator's voice here.
She addresses Maggie directly — 'Maggie Tulliver, you perceive' — and the effect is almost prosecutorial before it becomes tender.
The phrase she reaches for to describe Maggie's mind is wonderfully precise.
"In travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
'Travelling over' — as if the mind were a landscape, a terrain with cliffs and hollows.
And 'small mind' is doing something double — it's the narrator's fond irony, not condescension.
The very next sentence proves it: Maggie has deduced the meaning of 'poly' from 'polygamy' and 'polysyllable' entirely on her own.
That is not a small mind. That is a mind with no proper channel to run in.
Eleanor is quite right about the irony, and I would add that Eliot is making a point that touches something universal about the formation of character.
The phrase Eliot uses — 'the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams' — seems to me to describe not merely a child, but a particular kind of moral being.
The acumen and the blindness are not in opposition; they coexist, as they do in most of us.
What interests me more, frankly, is what the gypsy fantasy reveals about Maggie's will.
She doesn't simply sulk. She resolves.
Eliot tells us the resolution 'gathered' in her mind — as a storm gathers — and the scale of the scheme is entirely characteristic.
"No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more."
That exclamation mark at the start — 'No!' — is a complete character.
Edmund, you've put your finger on it — that 'No!' is one of those moments where the novel takes a breath and stands up straight.
As a performer, I adore reading that line because Eliot has already done all the work for you.
The justification for the gypsy plan is absolutely glorious: the gypsies would 'gladly receive her and pay her much respect on account of her superior knowledge.'
This child is eight years old. She has read the dictionary. She expects to be received as an intellectual celebrity among the gypsies.
And then the fantasy collapses with the most spectacular gothic speed.
Within five minutes of arriving, she has become convinced, as Eliot puts it with perfect deadpan precision:
"she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
'Gradual cooking.' Eliot could have stopped at 'kill her.' She added 'gradual cooking' for pure, devastating comic effect.
What I love about that passage is the theological joke that follows immediately.

Maggie suspects the fierce-eyed old man is actually the Devil in disguise — and she wonders, with what Eliot calls 'a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded,' whether the Devil would know her thoughts.
This is a child who is terrified and hungry, surrounded by strangers, and her mind races immediately to a point of speculative theology.
That is Eliot's method in miniature: the comic and the profound are never separate.
And it connects directly to what happens to Maggie later — that mind never stops asking the impossible questions.
I want to bring us to the darker consequence of that restless intelligence, because it seems to me the moral centre of the novel.
As Maggie grows older, that very acuity — the thing that makes her magnificent — becomes the source of her most acute suffering.
Eliot captures this precisely when Maggie recalls her earlier spiritual peace and measures herself against it.
"She used to think in that time that she had made great conquests, and won a lasting stand on serene heights above worldly temptations and conflict."
'Serene heights' — borrowed, I suspect, from the language of spiritual autobiography — and she has fallen from them.
What is so devastating is that her suffering is not merely her own; it extends outward, painfully, to Philip Wakem.
Eliot writes that recalling the insults flung at Philip was 'almost like a sharp bodily pain to her, making her beat the floor with her foot and tighten her fingers on her palm.'
That is empathy rendered as physical suffering. It is a moral achievement, not a weakness.
And set against that empathy, you have Tom — who is its absolute opposite.
I mean, even as a child we can see the shape of the man he will become.
In the opening passages, Tom simply transfers his preference to Lucy — and Maggie, who was Lucy's protector, finds herself contemplating actual violence.
Eliot puts it with one of her perfect comparative sentences:
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
The white mouse. It's almost unbearably precise — the smallness, the innocence, the fragility.
And now Maggie wants to pinch her. Because Tom.
The adult Tom, of course, is anatomised in one of the most extraordinary passages Eliot ever wrote about how a rigid mind works.
She is describing minds that feed on prejudice rather than truth — and she reaches for an image of extraordinary economy.
"Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye, — however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation."
'Give it a habitation' — the prejudice moves in, furnishes the room, and calls it reason.
And then Eliot lands the blow: it is 'at once a staff and a baton.'
A staff to lean on, a baton to beat others with. Two words, two functions, Tom Tulliver complete.
I find myself both admiring and resisting that passage, as I suspect Eliot intends.
Tom is not merely a vessel for inherited hatred. He is, as Eliot herself concedes, 'good, upright Tom Tulliver.'
The phrase carries irony, certainly — but it also carries a residue of genuine acknowledgment.
Eliot understands that the rigid character has its own form of integrity — the integrity of perfect self-consistency.
What Maggie suffers from is not simply Tom's cruelty but the tragic incomprehension between two characters each formed by the same river, the same mill, the same father.
Edmund makes me think about how Eliot frames Tom's prejudice against Philip — 'a meeting-point for all the disappointed feelings of family and personal pride.'
He doesn't even know what he's carrying. The feelings are inherited, like the mill, like the name.
And Maggie — who could deduce the meaning of 'poly' from two words in a dictionary — can see all of this, can feel it, can suffer from it acutely, and still cannot escape it.
That is the tragedy Eliot is constructing from the very first pages — the terrible gap between the range of the mind and the narrowness of the world it inhabits.
That tension — the vast inner life pressing against an unyielding external world — is, I think, the engine of everything that follows in the novel.
We've traced it from Maggie's childhood dictionary-reading and her gypsy fantasies through to the bodily pain of her adult conscience.
In our next segment, we'll follow that pressure outward — into Maggie's relationships, her choices, and the world of St Ogg's that will ultimately sit in judgment of her.

segments.title: Wit and Weather: The Comedy of Provincial Life

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've spent time with the novel's deeper sorrows — now we turn to something that often gets underplayed in discussions of George Eliot: the comedy.
The Mill on the Floss is genuinely, wickedly funny in places — and that wit is part of what makes the tragic undertow so devastating.
Oliver Trevelyan has been waiting for this segment, I suspect, with barely contained glee.
Oliver reads more Eliot aloud than almost anyone alive, and he's our guide today to the texture and timing of her humour.
Eleanor, as ever, will be watching what the craft is doing underneath the laughs.
And Sir Edmund, I'm told, has a view on whether comedy in a serious novel is a virtue or a distraction.
I have been waiting for this, yes — absolutely.
Because people come to Eliot expecting earnestness and moral weight — and they get it, they absolutely get it — but they miss the jokes.
And the jokes are magnificent.
Take young Tom Tulliver preparing his disguise — this passage from the early chapters is one of the funniest things in Victorian fiction, and nobody talks about it.
Eliot tells us that nothing but long meditation and preconcerted arrangement of effects could have enabled Tom to present so striking a figure.
The sheer gravity of that — long meditation — applied to a small boy with burnt cork and a red handkerchief.
But the real gem is this — and I want to read it properly because the syntax alone is a comic masterwork.
"Philip had once told him of a man who had a horseshoe frown, and Tom had tried with all his frowning might to make a horseshoe on his forehead."
All his frowning might — that phrase!
The earnestness of childhood rendered in the most affectionate, precise language imaginable.
What I love about that passage is the parenthesis — the way that horseshoe detail is dropped into the middle of a longer sentence.
Eliot uses the parenthetical structure to mimic Tom's own digressive concentration — his mind is completely, seriously focused on the wrong thing.
And the comedy is entirely free of cruelty.
We're laughing with Tom, not at him — because Eliot has given us total access to the internal logic of a child who simply wants to be terrifying.
He had amiable blue-gray eyes and round pink cheeks that refused to look formidable — refused, as if they have opinions of their own.
That anthropomorphism of Tom's own face is quietly brilliant.
I'll confess I find the comedy here something more than entertainment — though it is that, richly.
What Eliot is doing, I think, is establishing Tom's character through its most innocent expression before she places it under pressure.
That decision with which he grasped the sword — the same word Eliot will use of Tom in far grimmer contexts.
The comedy does not undermine the moral portrait — it inaugurates it.
Dr Johnson remarked that comedy is tragedy seen from a sufficient distance.
Eliot understands this perfectly — and she varies that distance with extraordinary control throughout the novel.
Edmund, that's exactly right — and it's why the satirical passages about Stephen Guest land so much harder than people expect.
The distance there is almost surgically precise — Eliot is inside Stephen's self-satisfaction and dissecting it simultaneously.
She sets up his endorsement of Lucy with apparent warmth — all those virtues — and then delivers the line.
"A man likes his wife to be pretty; well, Lucy was pretty, but not to a maddening extent."
Not to a maddening extent — that is a perfectly calibrated insult delivered with a completely straight face.
And the genius is that it's Stephen's thought, not Eliot's — she's wearing his voice like a mask she finds faintly absurd.
That passage is a clinic in free indirect discourse, isn't it.
Eliot inhabits Stephen's perspective so completely that the irony is invisible if you're not paying close attention.
He was conscious of excellent judgment in preferring her — and that word conscious is doing so much work.
A man genuinely confident in his judgment doesn't need to be conscious of it.
The word exposes the performance beneath the confidence — and Eliot does it in a subordinate clause, almost in passing.
I would not disagree with any of that — though I think we should be careful not to reduce the passage to a satire on Stephen alone.
Eliot grants him a genuine perception of Lucy's rarer qualities before she lets the irony do its work.
She says Lucy was loving and thoughtful for other women, not giving them Judas-kisses with eyes askance on their welcome defects.
That is not Stephen's perception — that is Eliot's own moral vision, placed quietly beside his shallower one.
The comedy is sharpest when set against that genuine standard.
And this is where I want to make a case — perhaps an unexpected one — for Aunt Glegg.
Because there's a scene late in the novel where the comedy and the tenderness become completely inseparable — and it involves Mrs Tulliver reporting back on a conversation with her sister.
Glegg has scolded, Glegg has been exacting and hard to please — we know all this — and then she says something extraordinary.
"I won't throw ill words at her; there's them out o' th' family 'ull be ready enough to do that."
In Glegg's dialect, in her syntax, that is love.
Eliot knows that comedy of manner — the vinegar tongue, the raisin-wine that turned out bad — is the outer shell of a genuine, sturdy loyalty.
And she gives us that revelation through Mrs Tulliver's breathless, slightly baffled gratitude — which is comic in itself.
That passage is one of the places where I think Eliot's ventriloquism is most complete.
Mrs Tulliver's voice — having she allays was, and hard to please — that rhythm is entirely authentic.
And yet it carries freight far beyond its comic register.
Because what Mrs Tulliver is describing — a shelter in her house — is precisely what Maggie has been denied everywhere else in the novel.
The comedy of Glegg's manner makes the substance of her offer land all the harder.
I think that passage illuminates something central to Eliot's moral vision in this novel.
Goodness, in this world, does not come wrapped in eloquence or grand gesture.
It comes in the form of Glegg's blunt, ungracious, entirely reliable decency.
And she'll give her good advice — she says — and she must be humble.
That condition of humility, delivered with Glegg's characteristic tartness, is nonetheless the condition of all genuine belonging.
It is comedy, yes — but it is also, quietly, the novel's ethics.
And then the novel takes the comedy away entirely.
There's a passage about Maggie's state of mind that stops you cold — I've read it aloud dozens of times and it never gets easier.
Eliot writes with this terrible precision about suffering — and the image she finds is extraordinary.

"The idea of ever recovering happiness never glimmered in her mind for a moment; it seemed as if every sensitive fibre in her were too entirely preoccupied by pain ever to vibrate again to another influence."
Every sensitive fibre.
After all the comedy — the horseshoe frown, the maddening extent, the raisin-wine — she takes us here.
And because she's earned the comedy, she's also earned this.
The fibre image is doing something very specific neurologically — not metaphorically, but almost physiologically.
Eliot studied the science of sensation — she was reading Herbert Spencer, she knew how nerves were understood in the 1850s.
And the idea that pain can so saturate the nervous system that no other vibration — no pleasure, no hope — can get through is almost medical in its precision.
It's not poetic exaggeration — it's the most accurate description she can find.
One finds, I think, the same terrible precision in the final image of the surviving mourner.
Philip Wakem — solitary always — finds his only companionship in a wood.
"His great companionship was among the trees of the Red Deeps, where the buried joy seemed still to hover, like a revisiting spirit."
A revisiting spirit — not a ghost, not a memory, but something still present, still circling.
And that, I think, is where comedy ends and something else entirely begins.
Eliot earns both registers because she never condescends to either.
The buried joy, hovering like a revisiting spirit — and from that image, I think we find exactly the threshold we've been standing on all conversation.
The comedy and the grief are not separate rooms in this novel — they share a wall, and Eliot knows exactly when to open the door.
We'll continue after a short pause — and when we return, we'll be looking at what the novel does with time, memory, and the pull of the past.

segments.title: Brother and Sister: The Crack in the Foundation

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the great English novels about childhood, family, and the slow accumulation of damage that passes for education.
With me are three readers who bring very different gifts to George Eliot's world.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher with a gift for seeing how great prose is actually constructed — the architecture behind the feeling.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as moral investigations — stories about character tested to its limits by circumstance.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novels than perhaps anyone alive — he hears this prose the way a musician hears a score.
Today's segment is called 'Brother and Sister: The Crack in the Foundation,' and we're looking at a cluster of passages from the novel's early books.
We have Mr Tulliver's anguished love for Maggie, the disaster of Tom's schooling under Mr Stelling, and the first charged encounter between Tom and Philip Wakem.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — with Mr Tulliver riding away from that farm, and then stopping.
This moment with Mr Tulliver is one of the most economical pieces of emotional writing in the whole novel.
Eliot gives us the physical action first — the horse checked, the head turning 'from side to side in a melancholy way.'
We understand something profound is happening in this man's inner life entirely through bodily gesture.
And then she delays the revelation — she tells us he is 'relapsing into the sense that this is a puzzling world' before she gives us the actual thought.
The delay is everything — it makes the line that follows land like a blow.
He turns his horse, rides back, and says aloud —
"Poor little wench! she'll have nobody but Tom, belike, when I'm gone."
That word 'belike' — the dialect word, meaning 'perhaps' — is doing so much.
It's not certainty, it's dread — the helpless speculation of a man who knows he cannot protect his daughter from the future.
What strikes me, building on Eleanor's point, is that Eliot is utterly faithful here to the limits of this man's emotional vocabulary.
Mr Tulliver cannot articulate his love for Maggie — he can only enact it, on horseback, alone, speaking aloud to no one.
There is something almost Shakespearean about it — the great feeling that can only find expression in plain speech and physical action.
Notice too that the passage is framed by his 'fit of promptitude' — he was resolved, purposeful, riding away on business.
And it is love that defeats resolution.
That is, if you will forgive me, the oldest story in the world — and Eliot tells it with complete unsentimental dignity.
I've read this passage aloud more than once, and I can tell you the hardest word to say correctly is 'belike.'
Because if you give it too much, you make Tulliver a caricature — the stage rustic.
If you give it too little, you lose the heartbreaking specificity of who this man is — a man who speaks dialect when he's at his most unguarded.
The whole sentence wants to be quiet — not whispered, but quiet, as if he's almost ashamed to have said it.
Eliot writes 'giving vent to the climax of feeling' — and that word 'vent' is brilliant.
It's not expression, it's release — something that had been building and could no longer be contained.
That containment and release is exactly the emotional rhythm of this whole section of the novel.
And it becomes rather grimly comic when we move to Tom's schoolroom — because what is being contained there is intelligence itself, under the regime of Mr Stelling.
Edmund, you've taught at Oxford — I imagine the Stelling passages speak to you rather directly.
They speak to me with some discomfort, I confess.
Eliot's portrait of Stelling is not merely satire — it is a forensic examination of how certainty without curiosity becomes a kind of violence.
The beaver analogy is exquisite — Mr Broderip's beaver building his dam three floors up in a London room, with no water and no possible progeny.
The narrator draws the parallel with beautiful, withering precision —
"With the same unerring instinct Mr Stelling set to work at his natural method of instilling the Eton Grammar and Euclid into the mind of Tom Tulliver."
'Unerring instinct' — the phrase is impeccably ironic.
The instinct is real; the error is total.
What Eliot captures is how Stelling's worldview is entirely self-sealing — a man who has never wasted time acquiring anything abnormal cannot conceive of what he lacks.
And Eliot does something structurally extraordinary in the passage that follows, about Tom's actual capacities.
She gives us this magnificent list of what Tom can do — predict cantering horses, throw a stone into the centre of a ripple, draw perfect squares freehand.
The list is doing double work — it's concrete, sensory, delightful, and it's also a devastating indictment of Stelling's blindness.
Then comes the philosophical digression on metaphor — and it's one of Eliot's most dazzling comic riffs.
She sets up the narrator's address to Aristotle as a kind of mock-lament —

"O Aristotle! if you had had the advantage of being 'the freshest modern' instead of the greatest ancient, would you not have mingled your praise of metaphorical speech, as a sign of high intelligence, with a lamentation that intelligence so rarely shows itself in speech without metaphor."
That address to Aristotle is comic in surface and genuinely tragic underneath — because Tom's intelligence is precisely the kind that cannot speak for itself in the approved way.
The cheese metaphor almost undoes me every time.
Eliot says Stelling's method turned out as badly for Tom as if he'd been 'plied with cheese in order to remedy a gastric weakness which prevented him from digesting it.'
There is something very English and very George Eliot about making a point about epistemology via dairy products.
But what I love as a performer is that the narrator's voice is visibly enjoying herself here.
There's a quickening of pace, a pleasure in the argument — 'It is astonishing what a different result one gets by changing the metaphor!'
That exclamation mark is earned — the narrator is genuinely tickled.
And then the delight shades back into concern for Tom — and you feel the tonal shift as something almost physical.
Oliver's point about the narrator's enjoyment is well made, and I want to add that it is precisely this quality — the narrator's refusal to be merely aggrieved — that saves the passage from polemic.
A lesser writer would have made Stelling a villain.
Eliot is at pains to tell us he had 'no secret belief that everything was humbug' — he was simply sincere in a very well-upholstered way.
The Swiss hotel-keeper who believes in the beauty of the scenery — that comparison is both funny and morally precise.
Stelling is not corrupt; he is incurious — which in a teacher is perhaps the graver failing.
Incurious as a failing — that sits rather heavily over everything that follows in the novel.
And it prepares us for the arrival of Philip Wakem, who brings curiosity so intense it frightens Tom.
Oliver, the first encounter between Tom and Philip — you've lived inside this scene.
It's a scene that requires very careful handling, because Eliot is doing three things simultaneously — and two of them are uncomfortable.
She is showing us Tom's prejudice against Philip's deformity with complete fidelity — she doesn't soften it.
Tom has 'a vague notion that the deformity of Wakem's son had some relation to the lawyer's rascality' — he has absorbed his father's hatred and attached it to a body.
And then comes the tailor — Eliot's great comic aside —

"There was a humpbacked tailor in the neighbourhood of Mr Jacobs's academy, who was considered a very unamiable character, and was much hooted after by public-spirited boys solely on the ground of his unsatisfactory moral qualities."
'Public-spirited boys' — the irony is almost cruel in its precision.
Eliot makes us laugh, and then makes us ashamed of laughing, in about four words.
What I find technically remarkable is how Eliot manages point of view in this passage.
We're inside Tom's perception — seeing Philip as 'a pale, puny fellow' with hair 'waved and curled at the ends like a girl's' — which Tom finds pitiable.
But the narrator never disappears — she keeps making tiny interventions, tiny recalibrations that tell us Tom's reading is limited.
'An anatomist — even a mere physiognomist — would have seen that the deformity of Philip's spine was not a congenital hump, but the result of an accident in infancy.'
That parenthesis is devastating — it quietly restores Philip's full humanity at the very moment Tom is flattening him into a type.
And then Tom walks across the room to look at Philip's drawing — that walk is the whole novel in miniature.
Curiosity overcoming prejudice — but only just, and only because he's bored.
And Philip's response to Tom is equally layered — he shows Tom his drawing, yes, but then comes the Greek history speech.
The narrator gives us the parenthetical gloss — and I rather think it is one of the most perfectly placed asides in the novel.
Philip says he should like to have been a Greek —

"I should like to have been a Greek and fought the Persians, and then have come home and have written tragedies, or else have been listened to by everybody for my wisdom, like Socrates, and have died a grand death."
And then Eliot quietly adds — 'Philip, you perceive, was not without a wish to impress the well-made barbarian with a sense of his mental superiority.'
'The well-made barbarian' — four words that contain the entire social and physical contrast between these two boys.
Tom has the body; Philip has the mind — and both of them know it, and neither of them can entirely bear it.
'A grand death' — Philip wants a grand death at about thirteen years old.
There is something both comic and genuinely poignant about that — Philip's daydreams are already tinged with a kind of grandiose melancholy.
And Eliot lets the fantasy stand — she doesn't puncture it cruelly.
She just tells us, drily, that he wanted to impress Tom — which is the most human thing in the scene.
We all know what it is to be the clever, awkward one in the room — and we all know the slightly desperate performance that comes with it.
That 'slightly desperate performance' might be the most piercing phrase for what Eliot does with both these boys throughout the novel.
What we've been tracing today is the architecture of damage — the way love, bad education, and prejudice all conspire quietly in the novel's early books.
A father who loves his daughter but cannot imagine a world that protects her.
A schoolmaster who teaches with unerring instinct in entirely the wrong direction.
And two boys sizing each other up across a hearth — one with a body, one with a mind, both already half-imprisoned by what the world has decided they are.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, and Oliver Trevelyan for an extraordinary conversation.
We'll be back with more from The Mill on the Floss very shortly.

segments.title: Social Currents and Moral Debts: What Society Demands

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been tracing the pressures — social, familial, moral — that bear down on the Tulliver household.
This segment turns to what society demands: respectability, duty, the performance of virtue, and what happens when those demands collide with genuine human need.

Edmund Leigh has been sitting with four passages that go to the very heart of this question — from the magnificent satire of Mr Stelling's ambitions to the extraordinary code of life Eliot ascribes to the Dodsons.
Sir Edmund, where would you like to begin?
I'd like to begin with Mr Stelling, because he is one of those minor characters who casts a very long shadow.
Eliot gives us this clergyman with his flaxen hair and his sonorous bass voice and his air — I love this phrase — of defiant self-confidence inclining to brazenness.
And she does something technically very precise: she never quite satirises him without also explaining him.
The line I keep returning to is this one — and it rewards being heard aloud.
"A clergyman who has such vigorous intentions naturally gets a little into debt at starting."
That word — naturally — is doing all the work.
Eliot inhabits the logic of self-deception so completely that we feel the satirical blade only after the sentence has passed.
And what makes it so devastating is that the logic is airtight within its own premises.
If success is certain — and for Mr Stelling, it absolutely is certain — then going into debt for the grand piano and the superior flower-garden is not extravagance; it is simply prudent anticipation.
The comedy lives in the gap between that sealed internal logic and the reader's external view.

And structurally, this passage is also doing preparatory work — Stelling will receive Tom as a pupil, and we already know that whatever education Tom receives will be shaped by this man's magnificent self-regard rather than by any actual pedagogic thought.
The passage is also a masterclass in the rhythm of satire.
Read it aloud and you notice how Eliot keeps piling clause upon clause — all those intentions, all those plans — until the sentence nearly buckles under the weight of Mr Stelling's ambition.
He would become celebrated by shaking the consciences of his hearers, and he would by and by edit a Greek play, and invent several new readings.
He had not yet selected the play.
That final clause — barely five words — arrives like a comedian's perfect pause.
The architecture of the absurd, rendered in punctuation.
But I want to turn from comedy to something that costs more — the scene where Tom addresses his aunts in the midst of the family's ruin.
Tom is fifteen years old, and his mother's words — the allusion to his father's disgrace — have cut him to the quick.
The narrator notes it explicitly: this was a remarkable manifestation of self-command and practical judgment in a lad of fifteen.
And then Tom speaks to Mrs Glegg with a directness that I find genuinely moving — even heroic in the modest sense that the word once carried.
"Wouldn't it be better to give it now, and pay the debt we're going to be sold up for, and save my mother from parting with her furniture?"
That is a boy speaking the language of moral obligation to people who speak only the language of respectability — and he is using their own logic against them.
What strikes me about that scene is the way Maggie is held in check by Tom — she starts up to defend her father, and he pushes her aside.
There's already the whole dynamic of their relationship encoded in that gesture: Maggie's impulse, Tom's authority, and the institutional world they're both navigating.
And Tom's practicality — which so often feels cold to us — here becomes an act of genuine love.
He is doing the thing Maggie cannot do: containing his grief in order to function.
I've read that speech aloud many times, and I'll tell you what's remarkable about it: the trembling.
Eliot tells us Tom speaks quietly and respectfully, but with a good deal of trembling in his voice.
She doesn't let him be simply stoic.
The performance of duty and the cost of the performance exist simultaneously in that single phrase — and that is what makes it audible as well as readable.
And then there is a single line from Mr Tulliver himself — brief, devastating — which I think contains more moral weight than pages of analysis could supply.
He is speaking to Maggie, who loves him as perhaps no one else does.
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
There is no self-pity in that line — or rather, what self-pity there is has been transmuted into something like wisdom.
It is the voice of a man who has understood, too late, that life does not extend the courtesy of second attempts.
That dialect — "my little wench," "twice o'er" — is doing something essential there.
It places him in his world, in his class, in his particular way of knowing things.
And the simplicity of the phrasing carries precisely the weight that a more literary formulation would dissipate.
You cannot improve on "I shall never live twice o'er."
Now — and I confess this is the passage I have been most impatient to reach — we come to the great set-piece on the Dodson code of life.
Eliot suspends the narrative entirely to deliver what amounts to a sociological and moral portrait of an entire class.

And she does it with a precision that I think belongs beside Burke's reflections on inherited social orders — not because the Dodsons are admirable, but because Eliot takes them with the seriousness they deserve.
Here is the sentence that arrests me every time I encounter it.

"Their religion was of a simple, semi-pagan kind, but there was no heresy in it — if heresy properly means choice — for they didn't know there was any other religion, except that of chapel-goers, which appeared to run in families, like asthma."
Like asthma.
The bathos of that final comparison is so precisely calibrated it makes me laugh every time — and then immediately makes me think.
That parenthetical — "if heresy properly means choice" — is the blade inside the velvet.
Eliot is using an ironic, almost scholastic aside to make a genuinely radical philosophical point: that most people's creeds are not chosen but simply inherited, absorbed, unquestioned.
And then she steps back into the satirical mode as if nothing happened.
The whole passage operates at multiple registers simultaneously — satirical, anthropological, and genuinely compassionate.
That last note is crucial: Eliot does not simply mock the Dodsons.
She writes that their pride identified honour with perfect integrity and thoroughness of work — and that society owes some worthy qualities in many of her members to mothers of the Dodson class.
The line that I can never quite get past is this one — about what the Dodson family motto was, and was not.
"To be honest and poor was never a Dodson motto, still less to seem rich though being poor; rather, the family badge was to be honest and rich, and not only rich, but richer than was supposed."
The gradations there — honest and rich, not only rich, but richer than was supposed — that is a comic ascending scale worthy of Fielding.
But it is also, beneath the comedy, a remarkably clear-eyed account of how a certain kind of provincial bourgeois culture actually works.
The secrecy of wealth is part of the code — not poverty, not ostentation, but the quiet possession of more than others assume.
And what unifies all four passages — Stelling's ambitions, Tom's speech, Tulliver's lament, the Dodson code — is a single, persistent question.
What do we owe — to society, to family, to the dead weight of inherited custom — and what does that debt cost us?
Eliot does not answer that question with a programme.
She answers it with people — complicated, self-deceiving, occasionally noble, frequently absurd, always recognisably human people.
And that — the novel's insistence on the fully human over the merely programmatic — seems the right place to pause.
Thank you, Sir Edmund, and Eleanor, and Oliver — there is more to come.

In our next segment, we'll follow Maggie Tulliver further into the question this discussion has opened: what it costs a woman, in particular, to navigate the demands of a world built on codes she did not write.
We've spent this episode tracing the education, the ambition, the love, and the grief at the heart of The Mill on the Floss.
And I want to close by asking each of you: what is this novel, finally, about?
Not its themes catalogued, but its deepest emotional truth — what it leaves behind in the reader.
Eleanor, let's begin with you.
For me, The Mill on the Floss is a novel about the cost of being exceptional in a world that has no use for your kind of excellence.
And Eliot shows us that cost being paid in the smallest, most ordinary places — in a schoolroom, in a failed Latin lesson.
Think about Tom at Stelling's — broken down over Latin supines for the fifth time, miserable, with nowhere to turn.
And the only recourse he can imagine is prayer — not confident prayer, but desperate, improvised prayer.
"and please to make me always remember my Latin."
It is almost unbearably tender — this small boy petitioning God about conjugations.
But what strikes me structurally is that Eliot gives Tom that moment of genuine susceptibility — she calls it the girl's susceptibility — precisely to complicate our judgment of him.
He is not the philistine we might lazily cast him as. He suffers too.
Eleanor is right that Tom is more than the novel's appointed obstacle to Maggie's flowering — and I would go further.
The scene that haunts me most is not the schoolroom at all, but the ruin of the family — and one sentence that Mr Tulliver speaks.
He has spent his pride, his money, his rage — and at the end he simply asks Tom to say no more.
"Give me a kiss, Bessy, and let us bear one another no ill-will; we shall never be young again — this world's been too many for me."
"This world's been too many for me." Six words.
That is not a social diagnosis. That is a man's final reckoning with his own defeat.
And Eliot gives it to him without condescension, without irony — with something very close to reverence.
That, to my mind, is the novel's central moral achievement — that it loves even those it cannot save.
Edmund, that line stops me every time I read it. Every single time.
There's a rhythm in it — "we shall never be young again" — that is almost musical in its resignation.
And as a performer, what you feel is the weight of everything that cannot be unsaid or undone pressing on that final clause.
But I want to bring us back to the children — because the novel's emotional centre, for me, is always the Tulliver siblings.
That scene where Tom drops the sword, faints, and Maggie shakes him by the collar screaming — convinced he is dead.
And then he opens his eyes, and Eliot writes — simply, devastatingly —
"She couldn't sorrow yet that he had hurt his foot; it seemed as if all happiness lay in his being alive."
All happiness. Not comfort, not relief — happiness. The word is exact and it shatters you.
And the brilliance is that the joy is inseparable from the wound — he has hurt his foot, and she cannot care, not yet.
That deferral — "she couldn't sorrow yet" — is technically exquisite.
It shows us the sequence of the heart in real time. Grief will come — but love arrives first.
And this is what the novel does over and over — it maps the interior with that kind of precision.
That is why we call Eliot a psychological novelist — not as a label, but as a recognition of genuine power.
And lest we forget, there is also comedy in this novel — real, warm, delightful comedy.
Maggie's time at Stelling's is not only about her brother's suffering — it produces this wonderful passage about Tom's expanded historical understanding.
Because Maggie asked Stelling so many impertinent questions, Tom arrived at a luminous idea —
"that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar."
The deadpan perfection of "the Eton Grammar" as the measure of human suffering — one could weep with pleasure.
Eliot is reminding us that even in affliction, she is also an incomparable wit.
Edmund, I could read that sentence aloud at dinner parties for the rest of my life and never tire of the silence that follows it.
And what I find remarkable is the emotional swing the novel asks us to make — from that exquisite comedy to Maggie shaking her unconscious brother by the collar.
Eliot moves between those registers with complete confidence.
That, to me, is the final argument for her greatness — not one note held throughout, but the full range of human experience, honestly rendered.
Edmund, Oliver, Eleanor — I think you have given our listeners everything they need to return to this novel, or to come to it for the first time.
A novel about intelligence unhoused, about love that cannot protect what it loves most, and about a world that — as Mr Tulliver tells us — is simply too many for some of us.
The Mill on the Floss rewards every return — and I hope this conversation has deepened what you hear in it.
Thank you for listening to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

c14:p58.text:
Maggie found the Latin Grammar quite soothing after her mathematical
mortification; for she delighted in new words, and quickly found that there was
an English Key at the end, which would make her very wise about Latin, at
slight expense. She presently made up her mind to skip the rules in the Syntax,
the examples became so absorbing. These mysterious sentences, snatched from an
unknown context,—like strange horns of beasts, and leaves of unknown
plants, brought from some far-off region,—gave boundless scope to her
imagination, and were all the more fascinating because they were in a peculiar
tongue of their own, which she could learn to interpret. It was really very
interesting, the Latin Grammar that Tom had said no girls could learn; and she
was proud because she found it interesting. The most fragmentary examples were
her favourites.  Mors omnibus est communis  would have been jejune, only
she liked to know the Latin; but the fortunate gentleman whom every one
congratulated because he had a son “endowed with  such  a
disposition” afforded her a great deal of pleasant conjecture, and she
was quite lost in the “thick grove penetrable by no star,” when Tom
called out,—
c14:p58.summary: Maggie discovers joy in the Latin Grammar's fragmentary examples, finding them imaginatively stimulating and delighting in the foreign language's mysterious beauty.
c14:p58.best_quote: These mysterious sentences, snatched from an unknown context,—like strange horns of beasts, and leaves of unknown plants, brought from some far-off region,—gave boundless scope to her imagination

c19:p18.text:
“It’s about Philoctetes, the lame man I was telling you of
yesterday,” he answered, resting his head on his hand, and looking at her
as if he were not at all sorry to be interrupted. Maggie, in her absent way,
continued to lean forward, resting on her arms and moving her feet about, while
her dark eyes got more and more fixed and vacant, as if she had quite forgotten
Philip and his book.
c19:p18.summary: Philip asks whether Maggie would love him as well as Tom if he were her brother, a question laden with the subtext of his physical deformity and desire for affection.
c19:p18.best_quote: Maggie, if you had had a brother like me, do you think you should have loved him as well as Tom?

c19:p27.text: “Oh, yes, I should think so,” said Maggie, laughing.
c19:p27.summary: Philip confesses his deep and enduring affection for Maggie, stating he will remember her always and, in unhappiness, will think of her and wish for a sister with her dark eyes.
c19:p27.best_quote: I'm very fond of you, Maggie; I shall never forget you. And when I'm very unhappy, I shall always think of you, and wish I had a sister with dark eyes, just like yours.

c19:p31.text:
“Why, I think you’re fonder of me than Tom is,” said Maggie,
rather sorrowfully. Then, wondering how she could convince Philip that she
could like him just as well, although he was crooked, she said:
c19:p31.summary: Wondering how to demonstrate that she can love Philip despite his deformity, Maggie offers to kiss him as she kisses her brother Tom.
c19:p31.best_quote: Should you like me to kiss you, as I do Tom? I will, if you like.

c15:p18.text:
Mrs Tulliver, as we have seen, was not without influence over her husband. No
woman is; she can always incline him to do either what she wishes, or the
reverse; and on the composite impulses that were threatening to hurry Mr
Tulliver into “law,” Mrs Tulliver’s monotonous pleading had
doubtless its share of force; it might even be comparable to that proverbial
feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel’s back;
though, on a strictly impartial view, the blame ought rather to lie with the
previous weight of feathers which had already placed the back in such imminent
peril that an otherwise innocent feather could not settle on it without
mischief. Not that Mrs Tulliver’s feeble beseeching could have had this
feather’s weight in virtue of her single personality; but whenever she
departed from entire assent to her husband, he saw in her the representative of
the Dodson family; and it was a guiding principle with Mr Tulliver to let the
Dodsons know that they were not to domineer over  him , or—more
specifically—that a male Tulliver was far more than equal to four female
Dodsons, even though one of them was Mrs Glegg.
c15:p18.summary: The narrator observes that Mrs Tulliver's weak pleading against law has cumulative force when combined with his fear of Dodson influence, though she is not powerful in herself.
c15:p18.best_quote: it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back

c15:p19.text:
But not even a direct argument from that typical Dodson female herself against
his going to law could have heightened his disposition toward it so much as the
mere thought of Wakem, continually freshened by the sight of the too able
attorney on market-days. Wakem, to his certain knowledge, was (metaphorically
speaking) at the bottom of Pivart’s irrigation; Wakem had tried to make
Dix stand out, and go to law about the dam; it was unquestionably Wakem who had
caused Mr Tulliver to lose the suit about the right of road and the bridge
that made a thoroughfare of his land for every vagabond who preferred an
opportunity of damaging private property to walking like an honest man along
the highroad; all lawyers were more or less rascals, but Wakem’s
rascality was of that peculiarly aggravated kind which placed itself in
opposition to that form of right embodied in Mr Tulliver’s interests and
opinions. And as an extra touch of bitterness, the injured miller had recently,
in borrowing the five hundred pounds, been obliged to carry a little business
to Wakem’s office on his own account. A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool
as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game! And it was vexatious
that Lawyer Gore was not more like him, but was a bald, round-featured man,
with bland manners and fat hands; a game-cock that you would be rash to bet
upon against Wakem. Gore was a sly fellow. His weakness did not lie on the side
of scrupulosity; but the largest amount of winking, however significant, is not
equivalent to seeing through a stone wall; and confident as Mr Tulliver was in
his principle that water was water, and in the direct inference that Pivart had
not a leg to stand on in this affair of irrigation, he had an uncomfortable
suspicion that Wakem had more law to show against this (rationally)
irrefragable inference than Gore could show for it. But then, if they went to
law, there was a chance for Mr Tulliver to employ Counsellor Wylde on his
side, instead of having that admirable bully against him; and the prospect of
seeing a witness of Wakem’s made to perspire and become confounded, as
Mr Tulliver’s witness had once been, was alluring to the love of
retributive justice.
c15:p19.summary: The narrator details Mr Tulliver's bitter conviction that Wakem orchestrates all his legal troubles and has humiliated him repeatedly; reveals his visceral hatred of the lawyer.
c15:p19.best_quote: A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!

c15:p9.text:
Mr Tulliver was a strictly honest man, and proud of being honest, but he
considered that in law the ends of justice could only be achieved by employing
a stronger knave to frustrate a weaker. Law was a sort of cock-fight, in which
it was the business of injured honesty to get a game bird with the best pluck
and the strongest spurs.
c15:p9.summary: The narrator explains Mr Tulliver's philosophy: he considers himself honest but believes justice in law requires employing a cleverer knave to defeat one's opponent.
c15:p9.best_quote: Law was a sort of cock-fight, in which it was the business of injured honesty to get a game bird with the best pluck and the strongest spurs

c17:p2.text:
All this, you remember, happened in those dark ages when there were no schools
of design; before schoolmasters were invariably men of scrupulous integrity,
and before the clergy were all men of enlarged minds and varied culture. In
those less favoured days, it is no fable that there were other clergymen
besides Mr Stelling who had narrow intellects and large wants, and whose
income, by a logical confusion to which Fortune, being a female as well as
blindfold, is peculiarly liable, was proportioned not to their wants but to
their intellect, with which income has clearly no inherent relation. The
problem these gentlemen had to solve was to readjust the proportion between
their wants and their income; and since wants are not easily starved to death,
the simpler method appeared to be to raise their income. There was but one way
of doing this; any of those low callings in which men are obliged to do good
work at a low price were forbidden to clergymen; was it their fault if their
only resource was to turn out very poor work at a high price? Besides, how
should Mr Stelling be expected to know that education was a delicate and
difficult business, any more than an animal endowed with a power of boring a
hole through a rock should be expected to have wide views of excavation? Mr
Stelling’s faculties had been early trained to boring in a straight line,
and he had no faculty to spare. But among Tom’s contemporaries, whose
fathers cast their sons on clerical instruction to find them ignorant after
many days, there were many far less lucky than Tom Tulliver. Education was
almost entirely a matter of luck—usually of ill-luck—in those
distant days. The state of mind in which you take a billiard-cue or a dice-box
in your hand is one of sober certainty compared with that of old-fashioned
fathers, like Mr Tulliver, when they selected a school or a tutor for their
sons. Excellent men, who had been forced all their lives to spell on an
impromptu-phonetic system, and having carried on a successful business in spite
of this disadvantage, had acquired money enough to give their sons a better
start in life than they had had themselves, must necessarily take their chance
as to the conscience and the competence of the schoolmaster whose circular fell
in their way, and appeared to promise so much more than they would ever have
thought of asking for, including the return of linen, fork, and spoon. It was
happy for them if some ambitious draper of their acquaintance had not brought
up his son to the Church, and if that young gentleman, at the age of
four-and-twenty, had not closed his college dissipations by an imprudent
marriage; otherwise, these innocent fathers, desirous of doing the best for
their offspring, could only escape the draper’s son by happening to be on
the foundation of a grammar-school as yet unvisited by commissioners, where two
or three boys could have, all to themselves, the advantages of a large and
lofty building, together with a head-master, toothless, dim-eyed and deaf,
whose erudite indistinctness and inattention were engrossed by them at the rate
of three hundred pounds a-head,—a ripe scholar, doubtless, when first
appointed; but all ripeness beneath the sun has a further stage less esteemed
in the market.
c17:p2.summary: Eliot reflects on the educational chaos of the pre-reform era, where incompetent clergymen like Mr Stelling ran schools as profit ventures, and anxious fathers had no reliable way to judge the quality of instruction their sons would receive.
c17:p2.best_quote: There was but one way of doing this; any of those low callings in which men are obliged to do good work at a low price were forbidden to clergymen; was it their fault if their only resource was to turn out very poor work at a high price?

c20:p18.text:
“Yes,” said Maggie, again faintly. Then, urged to fuller speech by
Tom’s freedom from apprehension, she said loudly and rapidly, as if the
words  would  burst from her: “Oh, Tom, he will lose the mill and
the land and everything; he will have nothing left.”
c20:p18.summary: Maggie urgently reveals that her father will lose the mill, the land, and everything he owns.
c20:p18.best_quote: Oh, Tom, he will lose the mill and the land and everything; he will have nothing left.

c20:p30.text:
“He’s at home,” said Maggie, finding it easier to reply to
that question. “But,” she added, after a pause, “not
himself—he fell off his horse. He has known nobody but me ever
since—he seems to have lost his senses. O father,
father——”
c20:p30.summary: Maggie reveals that Mr Tulliver fell from his horse and has lost consciousness since the accident, recognizing no one but Maggie.
c20:p30.best_quote: He's at home. But he fell off his horse. He has known nobody but me ever since—he seems to have lost his senses.

c11:p34.text:
Maggie Tulliver, you perceive, was by no means that well trained, well-informed
young person that a small female of eight or nine necessarily is in these days;
she had only been to school a year at St Ogg’s, and had so few books
that she sometimes read the dictionary; so that in travelling over her small
mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected
knowledge. She could have informed you that there was such a word as
“polygamy,” and being also acquainted with
“polysyllable,” she had deduced the conclusion that
“poly” mean “many”; but she had had no idea that
gypsies were not well supplied with groceries, and her thoughts generally were
the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams.
c11:p34.summary: The narrator reflects on Maggie's unusual, self-taught education: sophisticated in etymology and moral philosophy but naive about practical realities.
c11:p34.best_quote: in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge.

c11:p0.text:
Maggie’s intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined.
The resolution that gathered in her mind, after Tom and Lucy had walked away,
was not so simple as that of going home. No! she would run away and go to the
gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more. That was by no means a new idea
to Maggie; she had been so often told she was like a gypsy, and “half
wild,” that when she was miserable it seemed to her the only way of
escaping opprobrium, and being entirely in harmony with circumstances, would be
to live in a little brown tent on the commons; the gypsies, she considered,
would gladly receive her and pay her much respect on account of her superior
knowledge. She had once mentioned her views on this point to Tom and suggested
that he should stain his face brown, and they should run away together; but Tom
rejected the scheme with contempt, observing that gypsies were thieves, and
hardly got anything to eat and had nothing to drive but a donkey. To-day
however, Maggie thought her misery had reached a pitch at which gypsydom was
her refuge, and she rose from her seat on the roots of the tree with the sense
that this was a great crisis in her life; she would run straight away till she
came to Dunlow Common, where there would certainly be gypsies; and cruel Tom,
and the rest of her relations who found fault with her, should never see her
any more. She thought of her father as she ran along, but she reconciled
herself to the idea of parting with him, by determining that she would secretly
send him a letter by a small gypsy, who would run away without telling where
she was, and just let him know that she was well and happy, and always loved
him very much.
c11:p0.summary: Maggie resolves to run away to the gypsies after Tom's rejection, a fantasy she has long harboured as a way to escape family reproach and find harmony with her perceived wild nature.
c11:p0.best_quote: No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more.

c11:p35.text:
Her ideas about the gypsies had undergone a rapid modification in the last five
minutes. From having considered them very respectful companions, amenable to
instruction, she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon
as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking; the suspicion crossed
her that the fierce-eyed old man was in fact the Devil, who might drop that
transparent disguise at any moment, and turn either into the grinning
blacksmith, or else a fiery-eyed monster with dragon’s wings. It was no
use trying to eat the stew, and yet the thing she most dreaded was to offend
the gypsies, by betraying her extremely unfavourable opinion of them; and she
wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded,
whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts.
c11:p35.summary: Maggie's fantasy collapses into paranoid horror as she imagines the gypsies as cannibals and the fierce-eyed man as the Devil.
c11:p35.best_quote: she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking.

c37:p91.text:
Maggie went up to her own room to pour out all that indignant remonstrance,
against which Tom’s mind was close barred, in bitter tears. Then, when
the first burst of unsatisfied anger was gone by, came the recollection of that
quiet time before the pleasure which had ended in to-day’s misery had
perturbed the clearness and simplicity of her life. She used to think in that
time that she had made great conquests, and won a lasting stand on serene
heights above worldly temptations and conflict. And here she was down again in
the thick of a hot strife with her own and others’ passions. Life was not
so short, then, and perfect rest was not so near as she had dreamed when she
was two years younger. There was more struggle for her, and perhaps more
falling. If she had felt that she was entirely wrong, and that Tom had been
entirely right, she could sooner have recovered more inward harmony; but now
her penitence and submission were constantly obstructed by resentment that
would present itself to her no otherwise than as a just indignation. Her heart
bled for Philip; she went on recalling the insults that had been flung at him
with so vivid a conception of what he had felt under them, that it was almost
like a sharp bodily pain to her, making her beat the floor with her foot and
tighten her fingers on her palm.
c37:p91.summary: Maggie pours out her indignation in tears; she recalls her earlier spiritual peace and recognises that she has fallen again into worldly conflict. Her penitence is constantly obstructed by resentment at Tom's cruelty toward Philip; her empathy for Philip's suffering is acute and physically painful, causing her to beat the floor in distress.
c37:p91.best_quote: She used to think in that time that she had made great conquests, and won a lasting stand on serene heights above worldly temptations and conflict. And here she was down again in the thick of a hot strife with her own and others' passions... Her heart bled for Philip; she went on recalling the insults that had been flung at him with so vivid a conception of what he had felt under them, that it was almost like a sharp bodily pain to her, making her beat the floor with her foot and tighten her fingers on her palm

c51:p29.text:
But to minds strongly marked by the positive and negative qualities that create
severity,—strength of will, conscious rectitude of purpose, narrowness of
imagination and intellect, great power of self-control, and a disposition to
exert control over others,—prejudices come as the natural food of
tendencies which can get no sustenance out of that complex, fragmentary,
doubt-provoking knowledge which we call truth. Let a prejudice be bequeathed,
carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the
eye,—however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is
something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of
spontaneous ideas, something to impose on others with the authority of
conscious right; it is at once a staff and a baton. Every prejudice that will
answer these purposes is self-evident. Our good, upright Tom Tulliver’s
mind was of this class; his inward criticism of his father’s faults did
not prevent him from adopting his father’s prejudice; it was a prejudice
against a man of lax principle and lax life, and it was a meeting-point for all
the disappointed feelings of family and personal pride. Other feelings added
their force to produce Tom’s bitter repugnance to Philip, and to
Maggie’s union with him; and notwithstanding Lucy’s power over her
strong-willed cousin, she got nothing but a cold refusal ever to sanction such
a marriage; “but of course Maggie could do as she liked,—she had
declared her determination to be independent. For Tom’s part, he held
himself bound by his duty to his father’s memory, and by every manly
feeling, never to consent to any relation with the Wakems.”
c51:p29.summary: The narrator characterizes Tom's mind as rigid and wedded to inherited prejudice; his narrow imagination and strong will make him incapable of questioning paternal grievances or considering Maggie's happiness with Philip.
c51:p29.best_quote: Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye,—however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of spontaneous ideas, something to impose on others with the authority of conscious right

c10:p1.text:
Maggie said nothing, but turned away from her with a deeper frown. As long as
Tom seemed to prefer Lucy to her, Lucy made part of his unkindness. Maggie
would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty
little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but
then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been
left to Maggie to pet and make much of her. As it was, she was actually
beginning to think that she should like to make Lucy cry by slapping or
pinching her, especially as it might vex Tom, whom it was of no use to slap,
even if she dared, because he didn’t mind it. And if Lucy hadn’t
been there, Maggie was sure he would have got friends with her sooner.
c10:p1.summary: Maggie's jealousy transforms her affection into potential cruelty; she blames Lucy for Tom's unkindness and fantasizes about hurting her to vex Tom.
c10:p1.best_quote: Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her.

c18:p18.text:
Nothing but long meditation and preconcerted arrangement of effects could have
enabled Tom to present so striking a figure as he did to Maggie when she looked
up. Dissatisfied with the pacific aspect of a face which had no more than the
faintest hint of flaxen eyebrow, together with a pair of amiable blue-gray eyes
and round pink cheeks that refused to look formidable, let him frown as he
would before the looking-glass (Philip had once told him of a man who had a
horseshoe frown, and Tom had tried with all his frowning might to make a
horseshoe on his forehead), he had had recourse to that unfailing source of the
terrible, burnt cork, and had made himself a pair of black eyebrows that met in
a satisfactory manner over his nose, and were matched by a less carefully
adjusted blackness about the chin. He had wound a red handkerchief round his
cloth cap to give it the air of a turban, and his red comforter across his
breast as a scarf,—an amount of red which, with the tremendous frown on
his brow, and the decision with which he grasped the sword, as he held it with
its point resting on the ground, would suffice to convey an approximate idea of
his fierce and bloodthirsty disposition.
c18:p18.summary: Tom has elaborately disguised himself as a fierce warrior—or Bluebeard—with burnt cork eyebrows, a red turban, scarf, and sword, trying to look formidable despite his naturally amiable features.
c18:p18.best_quote: Philip had once told him of a man who had a horseshoe frown, and Tom had tried with all his frowning might to make a horseshoe on his forehead

c40:p64.text:
Was not Stephen Guest right in his decided opinion that this slim maiden of
eighteen was quite the sort of wife a man would not be likely to repent of
marrying,—a woman who was loving and thoughtful for other women, not
